title: ZenWell POC performance check-in vs baseline
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency and throughput results from Redwood lab runs vs the customer's current baseline provider. Discussed p50/p95 numbers, warm vs cold starts, batching/quantization tradeoffs, and next steps including targeted in-house run and security doc share. AE/SE recapped follow-ups and agreed on an extended in-lab test next week.
topics: batch size and batching policy impact
action_items: Maya Chen - Share full CSV of run results (per-config p50/p95, throughput) - 2025-10-24
Owen Patel - Schedule in-lab run for ZenWell with their dataset and 2x concurrency - 2025-10-28
Luis Alvarez - Send a sanitized 1k prompt sample for warm cache test - 2025-10-23
Maya Chen - Share SOC2/ISO audit pages + network diagram - 2025-10-24
next_steps: Run the in-lab benchmark with ZenWell's prompts using Redwood dedicated config A (quantized) and baseline provider configs
Compare cold-start sequential latency over 1k requests and warm cache p95 over 10k requests
Tune batching policy: test max_batch 8 vs 16 and report token/sec and p95 tradeoffs
Customer to evaluate cost-per-1M tokens estimates after Redwood CSV arrives
header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Time: 11:00 PT
Duration: 55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Rita Kaur (ZenWell CTO), Luis Alvarez (ZenWell ML), Samira Khan (ZenWell Product), Tom Becker (ZenWell Infra)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: OK hi everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off — this is the weekly POC check in with ZenWell. We've got lab runs to walk through and I think Owen's going to share screen with results.
[01:05] Owen: yep, pulling up the spreadsheet. Quick context: two configs we ran on Redwood dedicated nodes, config A is int8 quantized, config B is fp16 w/ dynamic batching. Baseline provider numbers are on the right, taken from ZenWell's telemetry last week.
[03:12] Rita: just so we're clear, baseline is the current vendor, they do 300-400 qps for us, p95 is usually around 720ms, p50 about 120ms.
[04:00] Owen: right. For our config A, p50 was 90ms, p95 420ms for 8-token prompt (avg seq 128). Throughput measured ~1,150 tokens/sec at concurrency 6. That compares to baseline's tokens/sec around 700 in the same test window.
[05:22] Luis: that's promising, can you say what the batch size was?
[05:30] Owen: default dynamic batch, we're effectively hitting batch sizes 6-12 depending on request timing. We also observed KV cache warmups reduced p95 by ~150ms once warmed.
[06:10] Samira: are those numbers from cold starts or after a warm cache? we care about worst-case for some of our synchronous endpoints.
[06:30] Owen: both. We ran cold-start tests (empty KV) and warm tests (preloaded prefix cache). Cold p95 edged up to 820ms on small early runs, but sustained traffic gave the warm numbers.
[07:50] Rita: hmm, that cold p95 at 820ms is similar to what baseline gives, but warm numbers are much better, which is good. Our product team cares about tail for first request user flows.
[08:30] Maya: yep that's where batching policy and pre-warming come into play. We can do a small edge cache or keep a tiny warm pool for your critical routes.
[09:10] Tom: question on cost — quantized config A looked cheaper in your estimates, how much cheaper per token?
[09:25] Owen: rough estimate: config A (int8) was ~30% lower per-token GPU cost vs fp16 because inference flops drop and we can fit more batch per GPU. We'll provide a detailed cost delta in the CSV.
[10:45] Luis: any functional regression observed with int8? hallucinations, slight decoding variance?
[11:05] Owen: minimal, we ran the validation prompts and saw 97.8% pass on the metric we use (semantic overlap); a few edge cases had token differences but not meaningful regressions for majority of prompts.
[12:10] Rita: okay. Can you also explain the p50/p95 mismatch vs baseline at higher concurrencies? baseline p95 stays flat but your p95 increases a bit — why?
[12:40] Owen: two reasons: we let dynamic batching run which increases mean throughput but can increase tail if bursts collide; second is kernel scheduling differences under high seq length variance. We have a tuning knob to limit max_batch and prioritize latency-sensitive requests into a low-latency lane.
[14:00] Samira: so we could have two lanes, one for realtime with max_batch 2 and one for background with big batches?
[14:15] Owen: exactly, and we can route by route or by header via your app. That keeps your synchronous endpoints fast while still getting cost benefits on other routes.
[15:30] Rita: security question: we need SOC2 docs and network diagrams for our procurement team.
[15:45] Maya: yes we'll send those. I'll attach the SOC2 summary and the VPC peering/network diagram.
[16:20] Luis: about the in-lab run — will you run with our real prompt set? we need the anomaly cases included.
[16:35] Owen: yes please send a sanitized 1k sample. We'll do runs with exact prompts, cold vs warm cache, and with p95-heavy sequences included.
[17:50] Maya: another item — baseline provider measurements were from their cloud region us-west-2; we matched region for fairness, but if ZenWell wants multi-region failover, we can test that as a follow-up.
[18:30] Rita: we'll want to check failover later, for now focus on latency/throughput and tail for first request.
[19:05] Owen: sharing a quick table: config A p95=420ms warm, p50=90ms; config B p95=600ms warm, p50=130ms; baseline p95=720ms, p50=120ms. Throughput: config A 1150 tokens/sec, config B 950, baseline 700.
[22:00] Luis: those numbers look good. Can we see distribution percentiles, like p99?
[22:15] Owen: we collected p99 but sample size for p99 is noisy in these short runs; we'll include p99 in CSV and note confidence intervals.
[23:40] Samira: how about cold-start mitigations — can you auto-warm caches before traffic spikes?
[24:00] Owen: yes you can schedule pre-warm jobs or keep a small warm pool. That does cost more but reduces first-request tail. We can model cost vs tail improvement.
[25:20] Tom: on networking, do you support private connectivity? we prefer VPC peering for the private option.
[25:40] Maya: Redwood Private supports VPC peering and on-prem connectors. We'll include the network diagram and options in the doc share.
[26:55] Rita: another practical question: what if model fails over to a cheaper variant — how are outputs different?
[27:15] Owen: we can enforce deterministic fallback policies with acceptable quality thresholds. In tests, the quantized variant diverged slightly on rare long-tail prompts; we can set A/B traffic rules so only non-critical routes hit fallback.
[28:40] Luis: we noticed one run where kernel scheduling reported a CUDA timeout in lab logs — is that something to be worried about?
[29:00] Owen: that was an anomaly tied to one host GPU driver mismatch; we patch those in infra runs. We'll surface logs and a remediation note. Not expected in production releases.
[30:15] Maya: quick recap — Owen to run in-lab with ZenWell prompts, Maya to send CSV and security docs, Luis to provide sample prompts.
[31:00] Rita: timeline? we want results before our architecture review next Tues.
[31:20] Owen: we can run 10/28 and share results 10/29 morning, that meets your timeline.
[32:10] Samira: any blockers on your side?
[32:20] Maya: only waiting on the sample prompts and confirmation to use a dedicated test pool; otherwise we're good.
[33:50] Luis: small nit — when you say tokens/sec, do you include the prompt tokens or only generated tokens?
[34:05] Owen: we include both prompt + generated tokens in the total tokens/sec measurement; we'll annotate that in the CSV.
[35:30] Rita: one more ask — can you include cost projection for our QPS target 500 qps sustained?
[35:50] Maya: yes, we'll include cost-per-1M token and projected monthly spend for 500 qps sustained with both configs.
[36:40] Tom: can we get a quick note on retry/backoff — if a request fails and retries, how does it affect batching?
[36:55] Owen: retries interleave with batching; we recommend client-side jitter to avoid synchronized retries creating large unexpected batches. We can provide best-practice client snippet.
[38:10] Luis: any security concerns around KV cache: is anything persisted outside the node memory?
[38:25] Owen: no, prefix/KV cache is in-memory per host by default; persistent cache is an optional feature and we wouldn't enable without your sign-off. We'll detail that in the security doc.
[39:40] Samira: are you able to do a demo of the low-latency lane?
[39:50] Owen: we can run a short demo but will need to configure the lane; we can demo in the in-lab run and include a short recording.
[41:00] Rita: ok, looks good. Anything else from Redwood?
[41:10] Maya: just that we'll include a short write-up about the tradeoffs we observed — quantization benefits vs rare edge-case diffs, batching tradeoffs, and recommended routing policy.
[42:30] Luis: and please tag the CSV with exact run commands and software stack (driver versions) so our infra can replicate.
[43:00] Owen: will do — we'll include run script, docker image tags, and driver versions.
[44:20] Samira: customer next steps internally: we'll run an internal risk review and share the sanitized prompts.
[44:40] Rita: procurement will need SOC2 docs, but that's tracked separately.
[45:10] Maya: great — to close, agreed next steps and timeline: in-lab run 10/28, results 10/29, docs 10/24.
[46:00] Luis: sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[46:15] Tom: thanks.
[46:30] Maya: end meeting.
[46:35] [call ends]
notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash) and speaker overlaps; timestamps approximate. Lab runs compared Redwood int8 vs fp16 vs baseline provider, customer requested sanitized prompt set and security docs. SE flagged a one-off driver anomaly in lab logs to be investigated.
